newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia scrambles to stave off U.S. sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Colombia scrambles to stave off U.S. sanctions.

text.p: Colombia signed a controversial anti-drug shipping agreement with Washington on Thursday, one day after beefing up its penalties for drug trafficking in a bid to stave off threatened U.S. economic sanctions.

The maritime interdiction accord allows U.S. Coast Guard officials to board Colombian ships suspected of smuggling drugs, something the United States had sought for six years but which Colombians saw as a violation of their jealously guarded sovereignty. Venezuela is the only other country on the Latin American mainland to agree to this.

Colombia is under intense U.S. pressure to step up its war against billionaire cocaine merchants and the maritime accord was on a long list of demands Washington made last year, when it warned that Bogota faced suspension of trade benefits and other sanctions if it failed to toe the U.S. line on drugs.

Other demands included passage of an asset forfeiture law to take wealth away from convicted drug lords, which was approved by Congress late last year, and stiffer penalities for trafficking, which were passed by both houses of Congress in back-to-back sessions on Tuesday and Wednesday.

U.S. officials cried foul last month when a Colombian judge handed down extremely lenient prison terms for brothers Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela, the top leaders of the powerful Cali drug cartel who once cornered up to 80 percent of the world's cocaine trade. The sentences could see them walk free in as little as five years.

The legislation approved this week would have prevented what U.S. have described as a gross miscarriage of justice, increasing the maximum penalty for trafficking from 24 to 60 years and cracking down on Colombia's plea-bargaining system.

The law is not retroactive so the brothers look safe for now, but Justice Minister Carlos Medellin says the government will move to lift Colombia's 5-year-old ban on extradition next month, which could clear the way for them to be bundled off to the United States where they face the likelihood of multiple life terms in a maximum security prison.

Officials led by President Ernesto Samper, who said on Wednesday that "Colombians don't need someone to pressure us to be honest," have bent over backwards to deny that they were cracking down on drugs because Washington told them to do so.

But U.S. officials scoff at claims that Samper or almost anyone else in his scandal-plagued government is acting of their own free will. U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robert Gelbard this week called Samper "a truly corrupt president" who had failed "to confront fully the drug interests that contributed millions of dollars" to his 1994 election.

Gelbard said it was only because Washington "decertified" Colombia as an ally in the drug war last year and because of "international pressure and the threat of economic sanctions," that progress was finally being made on the legislative front.

U.S. Ambassador Myles Frechette said the maritime accord and the law increasing jail terms for traffickers would be taken into account when President Bill Clinton announces next Thursday whether Colombia should remain on a list of virtual pariah states including Afghanistan, Burma, Iran, Nigeria and Syria that have failed to cooperate in the anti-drug fight.

Decertification for a second consecutive year could prompt stringent economic sanctions that Clinton stopped short of imposing last year. Frechette told foreign journalists the Clinton administration would also take into account a 30 percent increase in Colombia's coca production last year and the fact that drugs lords "are going like gangbusters."

Moreover, diplomats said that while Colombia's new anti-drug laws look relatively tough on paper, enforcement remains to be seen in a country with a notoriously weak judicial system where most crimes go unpunished.
